name: Costa Rica
verdict: Costa Rica does NOT have automatic jus soli for children of foreign parents. Constitution art. 13(3) makes birth in Costa Rica to foreign parents a right of OPTION, not an automatic entitlement: the child is Costa Rican by birth only if he or she 'se inscriba como costarricense' — is registered as a Costa Rican — on the volition of either parent during minority, or by the person's own act up to age 25. Absent that act the person never becomes Costa Rican and the right lapses at 25. Costa Rica therefore sits with the declaratory/optional jus soli group, not with Chile's unconditional jus soli — but the option is unconditional in substance (no parental residence, lawful-status, integration or language requirement, and no administrative discretion), so it is also not Germany's qualified jus soli.
instrument: Constitución Política de la República de Costa Rica (7 de noviembre de 1949), consolidated text published by the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones
reasoning: Four textual facts, all internal to the instrument, settle it. (1) Structural contrast inside art. 13: incisos 1) and 4) are flat statements of fact — 'El hijo de padre o madre costarricense nacido en el territorio de la República' and 'El infante, de padres ignorados, encontrado en Costa Rica' — with no further requirement. Incisos 2) and 3) alone attach a subjunctive restrictive relative, 'que se inscriba'. Inscription is written into two of four routes and omitted from the other two; on a formality reading it would be either redundant everywhere or required nowhere. (2) The operative words of 13(3) are 'que se inscriba COMO COSTARRICENSE' — registration AS A COSTA RICAN, a nationality entry, not registration of the birth event. Ley de Opciones y Naturalizaciones n.° 1155 art. 10, which implements this very clause by name ('En el caso del inciso 3) del artículo 13 de la Constitución Política'), confirms the two are distinct acts: the parent must 'comparecer personalmente o por medio de apoderado especialísimo ante el Registro Civil ... a solicitar que se inscriba a éste como costarricense por nacimiento', and the Registrar then, 'con vista de la certificación de nacimiento' — i.e. looking at an already-existing birth certificate — 'levantará el acta respectiva'. The birth certificate is the input; the nationality acta is a separate output. (3) The same art. 10 calls the actor 'quien optare por la nacionalidad costarricense' and the statute is titled Ley de OPCIONES y Naturalizaciones: Costa Rican law classifies this as opción, its own category alongside naturalisation, not as automatic acquisition. (4) The clinching internal-coherence point: art. 16 provides 'La calidad de costarricense no se pierde y es irrenunciable.' If the nationality vested at birth and inscription were merely evidentiary, the words 'hasta cumplir veinticinco años' in 13(3) would purport to extinguish by inaction a nationality that art. 16 says can never be lost. The age-25 cut-off is only coherent if what expires is an unexercised right of option — which means nationality has not yet vested. Registration is therefore constitutive, i.e. a substantive gate.
notes: Numbering caveat for the issue: the briefing assumed 13(2) was the foreign-parents clause and 13(3) something else. In the text in force it is the reverse — 13(2) is jus sanguinis for children born abroad to a Costa Rican-by-birth parent (also conditioned on inscription), and 13(3) is the jus soli clause for children of foreign parents. The atlas's 'parent_condition: registration' on the Costa Rica birth route maps to art. 13(3). | Gate content: the option imposes nothing on the parents — no residence, no lawful immigration status, no duration, no language or civics test — and leaves the Registro Civil no discretion (Ley 1155 art. 10 gives it only a ministerial role on sight of the birth certificate). So on a rights index Costa Rica should score well above Germany on gate difficulty while scoring below Chile on automaticity: the failure mode is parental inaction, not state refusal. A person born in Costa Rica to foreign parents whose parents never registered them and who lets 25 pass has no jus soli claim at all and must naturalise under art. 14. | Ley 1155 art. 10 still says the interested party may opt when 'mayor de veintiún años pero menor de veinticinco'; majority is now 18, so the self-exercise window in practice runs from majority to 25 per the constitutional text, which governs. | Fetching the source: www.tse.go.cr is behind Radware bot management and 302s a bare curl to validate.perfdrive.com.
